title: Studio Booking Sheet
story: A small recording studio keeps one booking sheet for its single room. Each line is a block of hours, like [13, 15] for 1 pm to 3 pm. The sheet is always tidy: blocks are in time order and no two blocks overlap or touch, because touching blocks get written as one.

A band calls to add a new block. Sometimes it fits in a gap; sometimes it overlaps one or more existing blocks, which then become one longer session. You need to rewrite the sheet so it is tidy again.
task: Write addBooking(bookings, newBooking). bookings is a list of [start, end] blocks sorted by start, with no two blocks overlapping or touching. newBooking is one [start, end] block. Return the new sheet: all blocks including the new one, sorted by start, with every group of overlapping or touching blocks combined into one.
Blocks that share only an endpoint count as touching: [10, 12] and [12, 14] become [10, 14]. Every block has start ≤ end. Return a new list; the input sheet may be empty.
constraints: bookings is sorted, and for consecutive blocks a and b, a.end < b.start

examples.explanation: [9, 10] ends before 14, so it stays as it is. [13, 15] overlaps the new block, and so does [18, 20]. All three together cover 13 to 20, so they become one session [13, 20].
The new block fits in the gap between 11 and 16 without touching either neighbour, so it is simply slotted in between them.

hints: In the first example, sort the old blocks into three groups by how they relate to the new block [14, 19]. What are the groups?

Every old block is either entirely before the new one (it ends before the new start), entirely after it (it starts after the new end), or it overlaps or touches it. Because the sheet is sorted, these three groups come in that order.
The blocks in the middle group all merge with the new block into a single session. How do you get that session's start and end from them?
Walk the sheet once. Copy blocks while end < newStart. Then, while start ≤ newEnd, widen the new block: newStart = min(...), newEnd = max(...). Append the widened block. Copy everything that is left.
bruteForce: Append the new block to the list, then run a full merge: sort by start and sweep, combining overlapping blocks. It is correct and short.
But it costs O(n log n) for the sort and ignores that the sheet was already sorted and tidy. Only the new block is out of place, so one O(n) pass is enough.

js: * @return {number[][]} the tidy sheet with the new block added
py: def add_booking(bookings: list[list[int]], new_booking: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:

tests.note: starts before the first and overlaps it

js: // 1. Blocks that finish before the new one starts.
// 2. Blocks that overlap or touch: absorb them.
// 3. Blocks that start after it ends.
py: # 1. Blocks that finish before the new one starts.
while i < n and bookings[i][1] < start:
# 2. Blocks that overlap or touch: absorb them.
while i < n and bookings[i][0] <= end:
# 3. Blocks that start after it ends.
walkthrough: The sheet is already tidy, so only the new block can cause trouble, and it can only touch one run of neighbouring blocks. Split the sheet into before, overlapping and after, in one pass.
Trace the first example: sheet [9, 10], [13, 15], [18, 20], new block [14, 19].
• [13, 15]: ends at 15, not before 14, and starts at 13 ≤ 19. Overlaps. The new block widens to [min(14, 13), max(19, 15)] = [13, 19].
Mind the comparisons. A block is "before" only if it ends strictly before the new start; one ending exactly at the new start touches it and must merge. The same goes for ≤ in the second loop.
solution.timeWhy: Each block is looked at once, in one of the three loops.
solution.takeaway: When one new item enters a sorted, tidy list, do not re-sort: split the list into the part before it, the part it affects, and the part after it, and only do work on the middle.
